The Pāśupata-Brahma-Upaniṣad.
"May there be well-being through our ears"—thus [ends] the peace invocation.
The First Section.
There are seven questions concerning the Controller of the World.
Now, indeed, Svayambhū Brahmā, desiring to create progeny, was born as Kāmakāma; Vaiśravaṇa is the Lord of Desire. Vaiśravaṇa is the son of Brahmā, the Vālakhilya.
He questions the Self-born One: "What is the science of the worlds? What is their deity?
Who is the god of this [universe] in the states of waking and the fourth (turiya)? Which things are under whose control? What is the measure of the times?
By whose command do the sun, moon, planets, and so forth shine? Whose is the greatness that has the nature of space?"
I desire to hear this; no one else knows it—speak it, O Brahmin!
I worship the state of Rāmacandra, which is the commentary [on reality], perceivable through the Pāśupata Brahmavidyā, the supreme imperishable syllable, and completely filled with supreme bliss.

Indeed, herein lies this Pāśupata Brahmopaniṣad, which is a division of the Atharvaveda; it is intent upon revealing the true nature of the Haṃsasūtra and culminates in the non-dual Brahman alone. Of this, [the following is] a brief [summary].
The commentary begins on page 228.

This narrative, consisting of questions and answers between the Vālakhilyas and Svayaṃbhū, is for the purpose of praising knowledge (*vidyā*). He introduces the narrative with the word "atha" (now). Now...

Immediately following the ripening of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) of living beings, the word *ha vai* are particles used for the purpose of recalling the subject matter of the preceding section. "He himself becomes," thus he is *svayaṃbhū*; Brahmā, having the desire "May I create progeny,"—the desire being a longing for objects of desire—was born, that is, he manifested. This occurred in accordance with his volition (*saṃkalpa*).

Kāmeśvara is Rudra; for according to the Śruti, "From the forehead, Rudra was born as Krodhaja," and so too is Vaiśravaṇa. || 1 || The one named Vaiśravaṇa, the son of Brahmā, the Vālakhilyas, and the host of sages attend upon the Self-born (Svayaṃbhū). Why? [The answer begins with] "What is the knowledge of the worlds? and so forth.
A sevenfold question has been posed. I desire to hear this from you; for indeed, there is no one else who knows how to speak upon this except you. Therefore, O Brahmin, please explain it. || 2 ||
The Self-Existent One spoke the answers to the seven questions: "The Vidyā is the mother of all worlds. (3)

The Oṃkāra, consisting of four mātrās—namely, that which is accompanied by two or three syllables, the mother of two syllables, and that which is accompanied by three syllables—is my deity whose essence is my own vital breath (prāṇa). (4) I alone am the sole Lord of the three worlds. (5) All the ages (yugas), as well as the times greatly increased by days, nights, and so forth, are under my control. (6)

7. My form is the radiance of the sun, and the splendors of the moon, the stars, and the planets. 8. The sky is my nature, consisting of the illusory power (*māyā*) of the three energies (*triśakti*); there is nothing else that exists apart from me. 9. Rudra consists of the *māyā* of darkness (*tamas*), Viṣṇu consists of the *māyā* of goodness (*sattva*), and Brahmā consists of the *māyā* of passion (*rajas*).
Indra and the others consist of tamas and rajas; there is no one at all who is purely sattvic, nor is there anyone who is non-terrible (aghora) and of a common nature. || 10 ||

Thus questioned, the Blessed One, the Self-Existent (Svayambhū), spoke. To what end? He dispels the first question—"What is the *vidyā* of the worlds?"—by stating that the *mātṛkā*, consisting of the forms from the letter *a* to the letter *kṣa*, is the *vidyā*, because it brings about the manifestation of the expansion of *vaikharī* speech.

He refutes the second question, "Which is the deity?", with the words "dvitrivarṇā" (consisting of two or three syllables): she who, in the form of a word, consists of two or three syllables; she is measured from herself as consisting of two syllables—namely the two syllables called *a* and *u*—and thus she is the "mother of two syllables" (*dvivarṇamātā*), while together with the syllable *m*, she is endowed with three syllables.

In accordance with the Vedic revelation that "this [syllable] is gross, short, long, and protracted," that *oṃkāra* which consists of four measures (*mātrā*) is this very deity of mine whose essence is breath (*prāṇa*). || 4 ||

He answers the question, "Who is the deity of this [universe] in the states of waking and the fourth (turiya)? with the words, "I alone. Of this triple world, which is characterized by the reckoning of states beginning with waking and ending with the fourth, I alone am the deity, because I am the mover of the triple world in the form of the *sūtra* (the thread of cosmic order) and so forth. (5) [Regarding the question: "Under whose control are those [states]?"

He refutes the objection with the words "mine" (mama). By the two words "the Kṛta and other ages" (kṛtādi-yugāni) and "also" (api ca), the meaning is that the entire world, consisting of both the stationary and the moving, exists under my control. He refutes the question regarding the measure of time—how long the periods are—with the words "day and night" (ahorātra). [The text continues: "possessing moments, days, nights, and so forth."

The periods of time extending to the end of the kalpas have been increased. He answers the question—"By whose command do the sun, moon, planets, and so forth shine?"—with the words "They are my forms":
"That splendor which, residing in the sun, illumines the entire world."
Know that the splendor which is in the moon and that which is in the fire is mine.

Thus, according to the Smṛti [text]. He resolves the final question—"Whose greatness has the nature of the sky?"—with the word "gagana. *Gaganaḥ* means the sky (*gaganam*). There are three powers consisting of Māyā, in the form of action, knowledge, and will, or in the form of Durgā, Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī.

The meaning is that the entire collection of its effects is the very nature of my own majesty. I am such a Supreme Lord; there is nothing whatsoever apart from me—thus he says, "There is no other" (nānya). [Verse 9] To the question, "What qualities characterize Rudra and the others?", he says, "Darkness" (tamaḥ). Because he is the destroyer of all...

This is because he possesses the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the quality of *tamas*. Apart from Viṣṇu, there is no one who is purely *sāttvika*, for he is of the nature of pure *sattva* due to his role as the protector of all boundaries. Therefore, he is *aghora* (non-terrible), possessing a universal form, and through the support of the quality of *sattva*, he exists in a peaceful form.
Because it is common to millions of devotees. || 10 ||

(p. 230) In the sacrifice of creation (*sṛṣṭiyajña*), there is the determination of the agent and other roles: Rudra is the creator of the sacrificial animals (*paśukartā*) for all sacrifices; Rudra is the deity of the sacrifice;
Viṣṇu is the *adhvaryu* priest; Indra is the *hotṛ* priest; Maheśvara is the Brahman priest who is the mind and the consumer of the sacrifice.
Brahman. || 11 ||

To the question of who the Rudras and others are, what they are like, and what they do in the sacrifice of creation (sṛṣṭiyajña), he says: "samasta... and so forth. In that context, Rudra is the "maker of the sacrificial animals" (paśukartā) because he makes the animals available for the act of immolation in all sacrifices, from the Agniṣṭoma up to the Vājimedha; thus he pertains to the sacrifice in general.

Rudra is so called because he is preeminent among the cattle (paśu). Viṣṇu is the deity of the sacrifice, because the sacrificial substance—the primary offering of the rite—is dependent upon Viṣṇu; as the Adhvaryu priest, he protects that substance by ensuring it is neither deficient nor excessive.
Indra is the Hotṛ priest because he is the impeller, acting as the one who performs the hymns and recitations (stotra-śastra) in the form of those respective deities.

Paśupati alone is the enjoyer of the sacrifice. "Mānasa" refers to that which is preceded by mental and vocal silence (*mānasa-brahma-vāṅmauna-pūrvam*). It is "mental" (*mānasam*) because, as the witness of the ritual performance accomplished by all the officiating priests through the mind, it augments the sacrifice. "Maheśvara" is *brahman*; for *brahman* is the witness of everything, and thus [it is] *brahman* [in relation to] Brahmā.
Know him to be Maheśvara. || 11 ||

The sacrifice of the contemplation of *nāda* is the mental *haṃsa*; "I am that *haṃsa*"—this identification with it is the sacrifice of the contemplation of *nāda*. The individual soul (*jīva*) is a modification thereof. || 12 ||
Regarding the question "What is this sacrifice?", he says: "It is mental" (*mānasa*).

The meaning is that the *haṃsa*—the contemplation of "I am He" (*so'ham*)—through long-term cultivation; that very contemplation of the *nāda*, which consists of that [reality] and is the means for attaining that state, is the mental sacrifice.

Thus, the living being (jīva) is the synthesizer; for as the mind fluctuates like inhalation and exhalation, the jīva undergoes modifications consisting of that [mind]. The meaning is that because the jīva has the vital breath (prāṇa) and the mind (manas) as its limiting adjuncts (upādhi), its state of undergoing those modifications is logical. || 12 ||
The Description of the Supreme Self as the Haṃsa:
The Haṃsa is the very nature of the Supreme Self. The Haṃsa moves within and without.
The Haṃsa is situated within, having entered into the spaceless interior, and is of the nature of the Suparṇa. || 13 ||

The *haṃsa* is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), for by means of the knowledge of its own true nature, it destroys—that is, it negates—the delusion of being something other than itself; thus it is called *haṃsa*. As to where this *haṃsa* ought to have its seat:
this very *haṃsa*, through its association with the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the prāṇa and apāna breaths, moves both internally and externally. Or else:

It moves within and without all living beings and is perceived as the form of Brahman non-different from the inner self (pratyagātman), for the Śruti declares: "Nārāyaṇa stands pervading all that is within and without.
Since desires and the like exist within all living beings, and objects such as sound and so forth exist without, this being the case:
Regarding the question of how it could possibly exist as either internal or external, given that there is no room for anything else to pervade it:

the *haṃsa* is the very nature of the Garuda who swallows the venomous serpents of desire, sound, and other objects, both internal and external to all living beings; it is the perfect knowledge that "I am Brahman, non-different from the inner Self."

The meaning is that because it is preceded by the dissolution of the conceptions of internal and external, the *haṃsa* becomes completely full by pervading both its own interior and exterior. And so says the *Smṛti*:
"The objects reside in the external regions, while the ego-sense (*ahaṃkṛti*) is within the body."
When all planetary influences have been completely pacified, it remains by itself.
Thus [ends the section]. 13.

The similarity between the *yajñasūtra* and the *brahmasūtra* is evident like that of the ninety-six principles (*tattva*) as threads: it consists of the three threads of consciousness characterized by pure awareness,
is encircled thrice by the nine principles, and embodies Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara, endowed with the portions of the three fires.

The knot of consciousness is the knot of non-duality (14). The swan (*haṃsa*), whose nature is Brahman characterized by the limbs of sacrifice, is the common limb of the sacrifice, blazing both externally and internally (15).
He states the similarity between the sacrificial thread (*yajñasūtra*) appearing externally and [the thread] appearing internally:

"ninety-six," etc. Just as the sacrificial thread becomes manifest as being characterized by the number ninety-six when measured by a span of four finger-breadths (*caturaṅgula*), so too [is it] characterized by the threads of the ninety-six principles (*tattva*).

The *brahmasūtra* becomes manifest. However, while the sacrificial thread (*yajñasūtra*) is characterized by three distinct threads, the *brahmasūtra* is characterized by the three threads of consciousness (*citsūtra*), consisting of the non-conceptual nature of the second and fourth [states]. Just as the sacrificial thread consists of three threads—

If that [thread] is wound three times, then it becomes a ninefold thread; likewise, the *brahmasūtra* also, when wound three times with the three options of two or four [winds], consists of the nine great principles (*mahātattva*).
Or else, through the divisions of the Fourth State (*turya*), Viśva, Virāṭ, Otrā, and so forth, it constitutes the nine principles.
It becomes threefold-revolved through the nature of the single flavor of *turya*, *prājña*, *bīja*, and *anujñaikarasa*, culminating in the third quarter (*pāda*).
Alternatively, the *brahmasūtra* is threefold-revolved by means of the nine principles (*tattva*), [pertaining to] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and... (p. 232).

Or it may consist of Maheśvara, endowed with the arrangement of the three fires beginning with Gārhapatya. Thus, the means for the unity of the Brahma-sūtra divided in this threefold way is that there is nothing whatsoever existing apart from pure consciousness (cinmātra) that is divided into three; this is the "binding of consciousness" (cid-granthi-bandhana).

Regarding the question of how the unity of consciousness—which illumines both the individual (vyaṣṭi) and the collective (samaṣṭi)—can be [attained] through the binding of knots: the "knot of non-duality" (advaitagranthi) is the knot of their unity, because it swallows that sense of difference;
thus, the meaning is that the knot of non-duality becomes the non-dual Supreme Self (paramātman). When—
The meaning is that just as the *brahmagranthi* of the sacrificial thread (*yajñasūtra*) is the cause of their unity, so it is here as well. || 14 ||

He states the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the outer and inner threads with the word "yajña": just as the sacrificial thread (*yajñasūtra*) shines externally and thus becomes a common limb of external sacrifice, so too the sacred thread of Brahman (*brahmasūtra*) shines internally and should be understood as a common limb of internal sacrifice.
The Haṃsa, however, is the nature of Brahman, characterized by the internal limbs of sacrifice. || 15 ||

The *brahmayajña* pertains specifically to the Brahmins; it consists of the sacrifices of the sacred verses (*brahmagā*) accompanied by the thread characterized as the *upavīta*. The sacrificial thread (*yajñasūtra*) is that which is endowed with the characteristics of being a limb of the Veda (*brahma*). That [thread] is the *brahmasūtra*. The *brahmayajña* is that which is connected to the *yajñasūtra*.
Its essential nature is that. || 16 ||

The external sacrifices, however, like the sacred thread characterized by the *upavīta*, have Brahman as their goal and are based upon Brahman. The sacrificial thread (*yajñasūtra*) is that which a Brāhmaṇa—endowed with the characteristics of the limbs of Brahman and endowed with the characteristics of the limbs of the Veda—wears. He alone also wears that *brahmasūtra*. How is this so? To this [it is said]:

The Brahmayajña is related to the Brāhmaṇa, like the sacrificial thread (*yajñasūtra*), because steadfastness in Brahman is to be accomplished by the Brāhmaṇa; for whoever is established in something becomes of that very nature. || 16 ||

The *praṇava* and the *haṃsa* constitute the Brahmayajña; the *mātrās* are its limbs. For the Manoyajña, the *haṃsa* is the sacrificial thread (*yajñasūtra*), and the *praṇava* is the sacred thread of Brahman (*brahmasūtra*) consisting of the Brahmayajña. The *haṃsa* resides within the *praṇava*.
The Brahma-sūtra; that very [text] consists of the sacrifice to Brahman (brahmayajña) and the sequence for liberation. || 17 ||

(p. 233) Regarding the question, "When one is established in the *praṇava*, what are its constituent parts (*aṅga*)?", [the answer is: the *mātrās* are the *mātrās* beginning with the letter *a*. Regarding the question, "What is the nature of the *praṇava*, which is the possessor of those parts (*aṅgin*)?", [the answer is: the sacrificial thread (*yajñasūtra*) is precisely the nature of that *Haṃsa* who shines forth as the fruit of the mental sacrifice (*manoyajña*), that is, the internal sacrifice (*antaryajña*).

The *praṇava* is the *brahmasūtra*, consisting of the *brahmayajña*. Since this is so, the meaning is that the *haṃsa* alone is everything; there is nothing whatsoever apart from it. That which is the *haṃsa*, perceived within the *praṇava* as the meaning of the *praṇava*, is itself the *brahmasūtra*.

That Brahman which is non-different from the inner self (pratyag-abhinna) is the *Brahmasūtra*; that alone is the *Brahmayajña*, consisting of the knowledge of the attributeless Brahman (*nirviśeṣa-brahma-jñāna*). That alone is the sequence of liberation;
for the liberation from the delusion of what is other than oneself, the means is precisely the knowledge of one's own true nature alone.
For any collection of means other than that is of no avail for liberation from it; indeed, this alone is the sequence, according to the Vedic scripture: "There is no other path for going. || 17 ||
The mental sacrifice (manoyāga) consists of the performance of the Brahma-sandhyā rite;
the Brahma-sandhyā rite is the mental sacrifice. The performance of the sandhyā rite is the defining characteristic of the mental sacrifice. || 18 ||

To explain what kind of mental sacrifice (*manoyāga*) it is, he says: "Brahman. The very identity of the inner self (*pratyagātman*) and the supreme Brahman—expressed as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) and "I am Brahman" (*ahaṃ brahmāsmi*)—is called the twilight rite (*saṃdhyākriyā*), the mental sacrifice.
For the twilight rite of those two is indeed the defining characteristic of the mental sacrifice; thus it is said here:
Through the knowledge of the oneness of the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman), their very distinction is shattered;
that is the true twilight (saṃdhyā)— it is not produced by ritual waters, nor indeed by the recitation of mantras.
"The union of the individual self (jīva) and the Supreme Self (ātman)—that is called 'saṃdhyā' by the wise," according to both Śruti and Smṛti. || 18 ||

The internal sacrifice is the contemplation of the non-difference between the *haṃsa* and the *praṇava*; the sacrificial thread is the *praṇava*. A *brāhmaṇa* is one engaged in the performance of the *brahmayajña*.
The gods move about in celibacy (*brahmacarya*). The practices of the *haṃsasūtra* are the sacrifices.
The non-difference between the Haṃsa and the Praṇava. || 19 ||
(234) The prayers of the Haṃsa pertain to the three times; the three times consist of the three phonemes. The external sacrifice is the contemplation of the three sacrificial fires (tretāgni).
The internal sacrifice is the contemplation of the syllable Om and the Haṃsa, whose form and phonemes are identical to the nature of the three sacrificial fires. || 20 ||

The nature of the fourth state (*turīya*) consists of that [consciousness], just as the nature of consciousness does; within the sun, the *haṃsa* is the nature of light. (21) It is the limb of sacrifice and the attainment of Brahman.
They practice meditation by means of the thread of the *praṇava-haṃsa* which is the activity of Brahman. (22)
He establishes the preliminary context to explain the non-difference between the *haṃsa* and the *praṇava*:

"The sacrificial thread (*yajñasūtra*)," etc. Because it indicates [the Supreme] as the sacrifice, it is the sacrificial thread; the *praṇava* is the *brahmapraṇava*, because Viṣṇu, who is the sacrifice, is the referent of the *praṇava*; thus, it is the performance of the *brahmayajña*.

The Brāhmaṇa is the practitioner of meditative absorption (dhyāna-samādhi) conjoined with the steadfastness of desireless action (niṣkāma-karma-niṣṭhā); he is so called because he knows the higher and lower Brahman. In accordance with the Śruti text, "The wise know that the movement of the mind toward the state of Brahman is celibacy (brahmacarya)," even the gods, such as Indra and others, are always [engaged in this].

They practice the holy life (brahmacarya), for they possess knowledge of Brahman by virtue of being disciples of Prajāpati. The sacrifices as well are the practices of the Haṃsa-sūtra, consisting of internal sacrifices—
namely withdrawal (pratyāhāra), concentration (dhāraṇā), meditative absorption (dhyāna), and samādhi.

Because it functions through the practices of the *Haṃsasūtra*, and because of the mutual correspondence between the *Haṃsa*—which is the self-mantra—and [the Praṇava], the non-difference of the *Haṃsa* and the *Praṇava* is established by tradition (*smṛti*), since the signified and the signifier are one. (19) To the question, "How is there oneness between the *Haṃsa* and the *Praṇava*? he says:

Regarding the phrase "of the Haṃsa": the prayers consisting of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth are the means for attaining the Haṃsa, who is the Supreme Self non-different from the inner self (*pratyagātman*). These [prayers] pertain to the three times, because hearing and the other practices are delimited by time. Indeed, the three times—past and so forth—are themselves the three phonemes beginning with *a*.
The internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*) consists of the continuous contemplation (*anusaṃdhāna*) of the three sacrificial fires—*viśva*, *virāj*, and *otrādi*.

How is that so? In this regard: the meaning of the syllable *oṃ* consists of the forms, phonemes, and configurations of the individual, collective, and their unified nature, which culminate in the non-conceptual states of the second and fourth [turiya] stages, pertaining to those whose essence is the three sacrificial fires beginning with *viśva*.
The *haṃsa* of the fourth-of-the-fourth state, which is beyond all comparison, contemplating itself alone as its own measure—this contemplation is the internal sacrifice. || 20 ||

Like the nature of consciousness in Viśva, Virāj, Otrā, and so forth, that [state] consists of them; it is established by the removal of the portions to be discarded residing therein, and is the nature of the fourth (turya) as distinguished within the fourth. Within the internal sun imagined by that [consciousness], which is the direct sun illuminating the mental modifications of desire and so forth within oneself, [it exists] in non-difference from that.
The Hamsa, whose nature is the radiantly shining light, is the Supreme Self. || 21 ||

Right knowledge— which consists of the internal sacrifice (antaryajña) characterized by the continuous contemplation [of Brahman]— is the means for attaining the primary goal, which is the realization of Brahman;
for the attainment of one's own nature is preceded by the knowledge of oneself as established through the impossibility of anything other than that self.

For this very reason, those who know Brahman and others, having first discarded outward activity, engage in an activity directed toward Brahman as non-different from the inner self (*pratyagātman*); the *praṇava* serves as its support,
and it exists in the form of the *turyaturya-haṃsa*, which is the object of that [activity] and which is incapable of sustaining the distinction between the inner and the supreme.

Because of the indication by a multitude of scriptural passages such as, "The fourth is illumined at the tip of the syllable Om; the fourth-of-the-fourth is Brahman alone, for there is no non-existence," and "In the Haṃsa-sūtra, not even an atom exists apart from Me," there is the knowledge of the undifferentiated Brahman. By that very [knowledge], the Haṃsa [realizes] "I am only Myself."
They practice meditation; the meaning is that, having such a culmination, they become identical with its very nature. || 22 ||

The seer Vālakhilya, the son of Brahmā, having spoken the ninety-six Haṃsa-sūtras, further declares regarding the Self-existent One: "How many in number are the Haṃsa-sūtras, and what is their extent? (23)
The station of the sun’s rays from the heart is ninety-six [finger-breadths]. From the nose of the thread of consciousness, the support of the *praṇava* has emerged for eighty-six finger-breadths.

Having thus understood from the mouth of Svayambhū, the sage Vālakhilya, in order to further consolidate his own understanding, asks about the extent of the Brahma-yajña-sūtra; thus it is said: "He spoke.
The sage Vālakhilya again addressed Svayambhū, saying, "O Blessed One, you [know] everything..."

He makes a formal declaration; because of your unrestrained omniscience, you have indicated [the truth] by way of leading one to the *haṃsa*, the Supreme Self. Desiring to know how many in number these *sūtras* are, what their extent is, and the measure of that [work], he spoke—that is, he asked. || 23 || [This is] the answer to the question.
The Blessed One said: "In the heart.

This refers to the state (*pada*), that is, the essential nature (*svarūpa*), of the rays of the sun of consciousness—which illuminate the existence and non-existence of the thousands of mental fluctuations such as desire—that shine forth within the heart and are revealed by the *Varāhopaniṣad*.
"Ninety-six" means equal to ninety-six cotton sacrificial threads (*yajñasūtra*).

Regarding where the rays of the ninety-six principles of consciousness (*cittattva*) have manifested: they have appeared in the heart of the Virāj of the Universal Body (*viśvakāya-virāḍ*), which is the locus for perceiving the thread of consciousness and the cause for the apprehension of the heart and so forth.
Having manifested through his volition— here, the vowel *ā* in "āghrāṇa" is a Vedic (chāndasa) usage— the principles (*tattvas*) emerged from the two nostrils (*ghrāṇayoḥ*, i.e.,
*ghrāṇābhyām*) in the form of exhalations consisting of vowels such as *a*.
Their divisions: as for the question of what their substratum is, they exist even today, having the *praṇava* presided over by the higher and lower Brahman as their substratum.
As for how many kinds there are, they are of ninety-six types, consisting of six multiplied by eighty. Or else—
They consist of ninety-six principles (tattvas), measured by ninety-six finger-breadths (aṅgulas). || 24 ||
The knowledge of the *haṃsa*-self alone is liberation.
The *haṃsa*, the Supreme Self, moves within the left arm and the right hip;
it is the secret mode of Brahman, known nowhere else. Those who know this obtain the fruit of immortality.
The *haṃsa* is not manifest at all times; there is no liberation without the nature of meditation on the *haṃsa* within the *praṇava*. 26.
The *haṃsa*, the Supreme Self, moves within the left arm and the right hip of this Virāṭ body; just as the sacred thread (*yajñasūtra*) shines extending from the left arm to the right hip,
so too does He pervade all the limbs characterized by the left arm and the right hip.

One's own ignorance, along with the entire collection of its effects, moves both within and without, through the various divisions beginning with Viśvaviśva and ending with Avikalpānujñaikarasa; however, in reality, the *haṃsa* remains as the nature of the Supreme Self, established by the total negation (*apahnava*) of all that. This is the meaning.

This matter, which is a mode of the secret of Brahman, is not known elsewhere, because it has been revealed specifically here alone. (25) He states the fruit of this knowledge with the words "yaḥ" (he who). One might ask: do all attain immortality—the fruit of that knowledge—by thus knowing the *haṃsa* as the Self? To this he says: "sarve" (all).

Revelation (Śruti) and Tradition (Smṛti) are my very command; he who acts by transgressing it is a violator of my command and a traitor to me. Even if he be my devotee, he is certainly not a Vaiṣṇava.
Thus, for those who transgress the path of the Śruti and Smṛti— which are the very form of one's own command established in the Smṛtis—
the Brahman alone, which is non-dual and of the nature of pure being, remains;
and even the entire collection of the state of ignorance and its effects, which are distinct from Brahman, is of the nature of absolute non-existence.

Since these two do not possess the relationship of signified and signifier, nor that of cause and effect, nor that of locus and located, [the meaning is: "know the *haṃsa* as the Self, which is always and at all times non-manifesting"—this is the ellipsis (*śeṣaḥ*). Of those...

The meaning is that because it is veiled by the fault of its own transgressions, the Self does not manifest its own nature, just as the sun is invisible to one who is blind during the day. He states that liberation arises from the cultivation of *sattva* and not from anything else: "The *praṇava-haṃsa*... etc.

The *praṇava-haṃsa* is the *turyātīta-haṃsa* (the *haṃsa* of the fourth state beyond the fourth), which is the meaning of the *praṇava* within oneself; [it is realized through] "I am That" (*so'ham*).
One whose nature is meditation, who is habituated to meditation, is liberated while living; liberation is within his grasp. Without him, no one else possesses liberation. || 26 ||

The superiority of the internal sacrifice over the external one has been examined in nine sūtras. They too practice that Brahman; yet the Āditya within has not been known by men. Having realized that the Sun of the world is the Radiant One (Rocana), those mortals...
The wise perform [this sacrifice] intent upon the prayer for the sun. Vājapeya is the one who takes away the animal;
Indra is the Adhvaryu priest; non-violence is the sacrifice of dharma; the Paramahaṃsa is the Adhvaryu priest;
the Supreme Self (Paramātman) is the deity; Paśupati is [the presiding deity]. Brahma is the Upaniṣad of Brahman.
Those who practice the life of a Brahmin are endowed with these two chapters. || 30 ||

Furthermore, those who regard the nine threads— mutually distinguished and proclaimed through their mutual differences as Viśva, Virāṭ, Otr, and so on, up to Prājña, Bīja, Anujña, and Ekaraśa— as the Self,
they too practice and worship that very thing which they call Brahman.

Because even those [limited beings] possess the nature of Brahman once the portions to be discarded within the ninefold group of all things have vanished; nevertheless, they do not know it as it truly is—thus he says "within. By humans, the nature of the sun of consciousness sporting within themselves has not been known by humans. Of them...

Because they are shrouded by their own ignorance. Wherein does their delight lie? The sun that is the Self of the world shines for them, because their vision is deluded by name and form. The meaning is that they fall away from the ultimate reality.
Some mortals and gods, having understood thus—

Those who are intent on the prayer to satisfy the mind that devours the darkness of what is other than themselves—born of their own ignorance—and who are habituated to the constant contemplation, "I am the sun of consciousness," practice the reality of the supreme truth. || 28 ||
Regarding what they practice, he says it is the "inner sacrifice" (*antaryāga*): "the *vājapeya*.
Because it drinks (*pibati*) the essence of food (*vāja*) that is distinct from itself, the *vājapeya* is the sacrifice of non-dual knowledge (*nirviśeṣajñāna*).

He is called the "Taker of the Fettered" (*paśuhartā*) because he removes the notion of "self" and "mine" regarding the body and other such things from those who are like fettered souls (*paśu*). That very Indra, who is accepted as the supreme deity, becomes the *adhvaryu* priest and acts as the director of the sacrifice of knowledge (*jñānayajña*). This is the reason for its superiority over external sacrifices.

This sacrifice of the dharma of liberation has non-violence as its essence. The Adhvaryu priest who carries out the sacrifice of knowledge is the wandering mendicant (parivrājaka) who is a supreme ascetic (paramahaṃsa). As for the deity of the sacrifice, Paśupati—the Supreme Self alone—is the deity. Such is the ultimate intended meaning of this Upaniṣad of Brahman.

It is Brahman alone and nothing else, because Brahman is the subject matter of the Vedas and Vedāntas. As for the question of who performs this practice: Brāhmaṇas who are devoted to their own study (svādhyāya) and have mastered the meaning of the Vedas and Vedāntas perform it, since they possess the primary qualification for the sacrifice of knowledge (jñāna-yajña). || 30 ||
The Horse Sacrifice (Aśvamedha) consists of the nature of the sacrifice of knowledge;
this is the narrative of the great sacrifice of Aśvamedha. Through that, kings practice celibacy (brahmacarya).
For all of them, the aforementioned sequence of the Brahma-sacrifice is the sequence of liberation. || 31 ||

Regarding the nature of the discourse on the *mahāyajña*: the "fattening of the sacrificial animal" (*paśumedhana*) refers to the slaughter (*viśasana*), which is its negation (*apahnava*); and the "horse-sacrifice" (*aśvamedha*), which is unworthy of trust as it might occur tomorrow or the day after, occurs at the very moment of one's own realization.
For it is logical to negate anything that is other than and general to one's own Self;
indeed, this very discourse on the great sacrifice of non-dual supreme knowledge (*nirviśeṣa-mahājñāna-yajña*) is what is meant by "renown" (*khyāti*).
In such a great horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha-mahāyajña*), one shines as nothing but one's own Self, which is devoid of all counter-correlates (*niṣpratiyogika-svamātra*).
Those who have been favored by that king through his own performance of the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*),
thinking "may they become successful," practice the two-fold celibacy (*brahmacarya*),
because for those excluded from his grace, such [attainment] is extremely difficult to obtain; this is what applies to all of them.

Know that for those seeking liberation, the path that leads to the attainment of Brahman is this aforementioned sequence of the Brahma-sacrifice (brahmayajña) and the sequence of liberation (muktikrama). || 31 ||

The son of Brahmā, Tārakahaṃsajyotis, spoke: "The sage Haṃsa has arisen; Svayambhū has vanished. Rudra is the Brahmopaniṣad; Paśupati is the Haṃsajyotis; he is the Praṇava, the Tāraka—he who knows thus."
Thus favored by the Self-born (Svayaṃbhū), the son of Brahmā, the host of Vālakhilyas, spoke. What did he say? "By the power of the Blessed One’s instruction, the Ṛṣi Haṃsa has arisen;
as the Haṃsa who is established through the negation of everything else, he is the Supreme Self (Paramātman) as one's own nature alone, free from all opposition."

Having heard the disciple’s words, "He has appeared; therefore, I have accomplished my purpose," the Self-born One (Svayambhū), being exceedingly delighted, vanished—meaning he returned to his own essential nature. He states that Rudra and Vaiśravaṇa also know this thus: "Rudra. Along with Vaiśravaṇa, Rudra as well [knows it].

The meaning is that Paśupati, through the mouth of the Self-Existent (Svayaṃbhū), understood the supreme intention of the Brahmopaniṣad—the purpose of the Brahmatāraka—namely, "I am the light of the Haṃsa. || 32 ||
The Uttarakaṇḍa is the attainment of Brahman through uninterrupted function;
it is the garland of the self as the Swan (Haṃsa), impelled by the time of the phonemic Brahman.
The Supreme Self is the Person; this is the narrative that brings about union with Brahman.
What kind of discourse is there for one who is like the Brahman of the inner self? 1.

To explain how he knew this, he says: "The swan," etc. This syllable *oṃ*, which consists of the letters of the *mālā* and is of the nature of the designator (*abhidhāna*), is the very Brahman—which is the nature of the designated object (*abhidheya*) and the self of the swan—having attained the form of Kāleśvara, it is thus...

He is the impeller, the prompter, and the instigator who urges all living beings toward what is beneficial and what is harmful, saying, "This must be done" and "This must not be done. Yet, in His own true nature, the Person, the Lord—when the distinctions inherent in Him have vanished—is the non-dual Supreme Self, remaining as His own essence alone. This is the meaning.

The modification (*vṛtti*) of consciousness in the form of an undivided whole arises; this very [modification] brings about the attainment of Brahman, and thus it is "that which effects the attainment of Brahman.

It is this very [modification], well-known in the Vedānta through such texts as "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself," that constitutes the form for the realization of the internal Brahman-creation.
The meaning is that it is an unrestrained means. To strengthen the stated point, he raises an objection as follows: "What kind of story is it? (1)
The manifestation of the world in the Supreme Self is illusory (*māyika*).
For the wise, the time of twilight is the radiance of the knowledge of Brahman.
How can the progeny of the *ātmatattva*, known as the Divine Swan (*haṃsa*), [perceive] the Self? (2)
Within, the *haṃsa*—known as the sound of the *praṇava*—is the awakener of realization;
it shines forth as the stalk of knowledge, hidden within the measure of the inner self. (3)
The form consisting of Śiva and Śakti is known as the bliss of pure consciousness;
it comprises the three—Nāda, Bindu, and Kalā—and is the universal activity of the Eye.
The three parts are the crest, numbering three and two;
its form is hidden within, while the *haṃsa* emerges from the measurement outward.

Regarding the question of what kind of discourse concerns the mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of Brahman: the radiance of the sun that is the knowledge of Brahman brings about the unity of the realization of the inner consciousness and the outer consciousness; therefore, it is called *saṃdhyā* (the junction). Indeed, by means of this, time passes for the wise who are liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*). For those liberated while living...
Because time has been destroyed by the non-dual samādhi of Brahman,

if one worships the inner deity— the Supreme Self, which is the self-luminous pure consciousness— known as the *haṃsa* that swallows the external phenomenal world beyond oneself, then [one abides] in the reality of one's own Self.

"How is the progeny, such as Viśva, Virāṭ, and Otrā, born?"— regarding this, [the author] says "internally" (antar), explaining that from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārthataḥ), no progeny whatsoever is born apart from the Self; however, when [the Self], through Māyā, appears by assuming the state of the inner witness (pratyak) and so forth, then the entire range of objects to be manifested also appears as if born.

In the Nāradaparivrājaka Upaniṣad, the internal *praṇava* consisting of eight measures (*mātrā*) is thoroughly expounded. Therein, within the resonance (*nāda*) of the internal *praṇava*, the inward-facing *haṃsa* becomes the illuminator;
it is the illuminator that makes known the entire collection of outward-directed conceptual cognitions (*vikalpita-parāk-pratyaya-kadamba*) imagined within and without oneself.

If that is so, why is that inner reality not perceived? To this [it is said]: For those who perceive through the external [senses], it shines hidden within their cognition; yet, from the perspective of that [inner] vision, it appears as the stalk of knowledge in the form of the immediate consciousness that illumines all.
"It is not capable of being manifested, not capable"—the meaning is that it does not exist as if it were something capable [of being known by another].
What is that which is non-luminous in nature? To this: "It shines by its own form," because, through its self-luminosity, it is the illuminator of all. (3) By whom is it thus known? To this:

That which is of the nature of Śiva and Śakti, appearing as a variegated form to those with outward vision, becomes known as "I am Existence-Consciousness-Bliss" (saccidānanda) by the removal of the portions consisting of internal particularities; regarding this, it is said:
"This Self, hidden in all beings, does not shine forth."
But it is seen by those of subtle vision with a sharp and subtle intellect.

Thus says the Śruti. Furthermore, from the perspective of one who lacks self-knowledge (*svājña-dṛṣṭi*), there are the three components of the *praṇava*—namely *nāda*, *bindu*, and *kalā*—and their effects: the three powers of grace (*anugraha*), withdrawal (*upasaṃhāra*), and concealment (*tirodhāna*), presided over by Sadāśiva and the others. This entire collection of conceptual constructs is the Viśva, located in the opening of the right eye.

And as for the statement, "One should know that the waking state resides in the eyes," the meaning is that the activity of Viśva—the ego who identifies with the waking state produced by the fourteen instruments beginning with the eyes, which are established by scripture—is merely a mental construction (vikalpita). || 4 ||

Regarding the question of what various things have been conceptualized by Viśva: there are three types of bodies distinguished as gross, subtle, and causal; the forms of the peaks known as Viśva, Taijasa, and Prājña mounted upon them;
and the three groups of five—the five elements, their effects, and the elemental derivatives—which are thus enumerated.

The meaning is that all designators of number, everywhere—whether explicitly mentioned or unmentioned, whether forms or modifications of name-and-form—are all conceptualized by one's own ignorance regarding the universe. Thus, when the conceptualizations pertaining to this world of conceptualizers cease, that very reality becomes manifest; he says "within" (antar) to express this.

That which previously existed as the *haṃsa* hidden within the form of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) of all living beings— as established by scriptural authority such as "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite"— is now the reality of Brahman, non-different from the inner self (*pratyagātman*), which has emerged and become manifest externally. Since it is thus...
One should meditate upon that very Self, which is established by the authority of the Vedas, as the non-dual Brahman, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss. || 5 ||
The method of meditation on the Haṃsa, Arka,
and Praṇava is to be known as the state of the Brahma-sūtra, characterized by the injunctions of the Veda;
this is called "meditation on the Haṃsa, Arka, and Praṇava" in the Jñānasāgara.
By the mere realization of this, one reaches the further shore of the ocean of knowledge;

through the statement "I am Brahman," which possesses the characteristics described in the scriptural texts that negate the appearance of injunctions, one knows the Self alone— that which pertains to Brahman.

It is known as the *Brahmasūtra* because it indicates [reality] through its being nothing but Brahman; it is called a *pada* (foot/step) because it leads to that which remains as one's own self; and it is to be understood as expanding in a state of eternal uniformity.
Thus, he who performs the meditation on the *haṃsa*, the sun, and the *praṇava* enters into Brahman, the ocean of knowledge.
It is said that [liberation] becomes accomplished. Whoever is a seeker of liberation,

by the mere knowledge "I am Brahman" characterized as described above, reaches the shore of the ocean of delusion consisting of knowledge, ignorance, and their effects— which manifest internally and externally as something other than oneself— and abides as the non-dual Brahman alone, which is without a counterpart.
The meaning is that it arises from the kaivalya (isolation) of the body which is devoid of the characteristics of persistence.
The Supreme Consciousness alone is the impeller of the instruments; Śiva, the Lord of Creatures, is himself the witness of everything at all times.
However, when the mind of all is impelled by that [breath] according to its rule, it moves toward the sense objects; the vital breath (prāṇa) exerts itself, and speech also speaks.
The eye sees forms, and the ear hears everything; all the other sense-voids (ākāśas) are indeed impelled by that very same [principle].
They proceed incessantly, each directed toward its own respective object;
and this capacity for setting [them] in motion belongs to it through *māyā*, not by its own nature.
The Supreme Lord Paśupati himself, the Person Śiva, having entered into the ear which is superimposed upon the Self, bestows the state of being the sense of hearing upon that ear. 11.
Having entered the mind that is superimposed upon his own self, the Supreme Lord,
abiding in the state of pure being (sattva), bestows the nature of "mind-ness" upon it by means of his constant discipline.
He alone is other than the known, and likewise other than the unknown;
He is the Lord even of the other [five] sense organs, though they are merely conceptualized. (13)
Having assumed each respective form, [the Self] bestows [its effects] according to rule. (p.
243) But when the collection of organs is merely a reality imagined by one's own ignorance (*svājñā-vikalpita*), who is its mover?

To this he says: "By itself" (*svataḥ*). (7) "In their respective objects" (*svasva-viṣaye*). (8–9) Not by way of inherent nature (*svabhāva*), because it is by nature changeless (*nirvikāra*). (10–12)

If it be argued that [the Self] is the instrument itself and the driver of the collection of instruments, then it would follow that this [Self] is a transmigrating being (saṃsārī); anticipating this objection, he says "He alone" to show that because of the absence of the conceit of "I" and "mine," and because of being distinct from that [collection], it is not a transmigrating being. He who, while being the very nature of the collection of instruments, is also their driver—[he alone is the Lord].
Thus [it is]. || 13–14 ||
The self and that which is other than it are both fashioned by māyā; therefore, the eye, speech, the mind, and the other sense-voids [are likewise so fashioned]. 14.

They do not go [to the state of liberation] within the Supreme Self, whose nature is self-luminous; rather, it is manifested by its own self as an immediate light, free from agency and objective content. 15.
The meaning is that this has been fully elaborated in the *Kenopaniṣad* with such statements as, "He who knows Brahman without [relying on] reasoning and means of valid cognition—he truly knows.

Because they belong to the same context, he says—referring to the phrase "having as its object the non-agent"—that even the nature of being the inner self (*pratyaktva*) is illusory (*māyika*). || 15 ||
In reality, the possibility of illusion within one's own self pertains to the innermost Self (pratyagātman), which is the supreme light; that illusion, however, is the Great Darkness (mahattamas).
If that were so, how could illusion arise within the inner self?
Therefore, by means of reasoning, valid cognition, and one's own direct experience, [one realizes] the density of consciousness.
In the Supreme Self, which is established solely as self-luminous, there is no māyā;
this distinction between knowledge and ignorance exists only from the perspective of empirical convention, and not otherwise. (18)
(244) From the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvadṛṣṭi*), however, there is no such thing as reality at all; only the Absolute (*kevala*) exists.
But from the conventional perspective (*vyāvahārikadṛṣṭi*), [reality] exists because it is never dissociated from manifestation (*prakāśa*). (19)
Therefore, it is indeed always only light; for non-duality (advaita) exists precisely because even the expression "non-duality" does not deviate from that light.
Therefore, since [the Self] is eternally light itself, silence is indeed appropriate.
He states that, in reality, the appearance of māyā within one's own Self is as follows: "The innermost... (verse 16).

Since this is so, therefore [verses 17–18]. He states that even the conventional perspective does not exist apart from the Self—“the conventional,” etc. (verse 19). He states that even the expression “non-duality” is not ultimately real—“non-duality,” etc.; for the expression “non-duality” is dependent upon its opposite, duality. (verse 20)
For the knower of the Self, this great truth—that one's very self is Brahman—is revealed by itself. || 21 ||
He is neither the individual soul (jīva) nor Brahmā, nor anything else whatsoever;
for him, no castes exist, and likewise no stages of life (āśramas).
For him there is neither dharma nor adharma, neither prohibition nor injunction, when everything shines forth by its own nature as being of the essence of Brahman. (23)
At that time, even this appearance of the distinctions of suffering and so forth does not manifest;
for the knower of the supreme Self, though perceiving [the world] in the form of the universe, living beings, and so on, [sees it as such].
That which is of the nature of consciousness does not see that [object]; it sees only the reality of Brahman.
Indeed, the discourse of "attribute" and "substratum" is distinguished only when there is difference.
Difference, non-difference, and likewise both difference and non-difference belong directly to the Supreme Self;
apart from its own nature, it does not exist, for it exists by itself alone at all times. (26)
Brahman alone exists directly, both as a reality and as an unreality;
likewise, the knower of Brahman—what does he grasp, and what does he abandon? (27)
The foundation is incomparable, beyond the range of speech and mind;
that which is invisible, ungraspable, without lineage, and devoid of form. (28)
It is without eyes or ears, and likewise without hands or feet;
it is eternal, all-pervading, omnipresent, exceedingly subtle, and imperishable.
This immortal Brahman alone is in the east;
the supreme bliss of Brahman is indeed in the west;
and the supreme bliss of Brahman is in the south.
The supreme and ultimate bliss of Brahman. || 30 ||
When one always perceives everything within one's own self by oneself, free from fear, then one is liberated;
yet one is not [merely] liberated, for liberation belongs only to that which was bound. (31)

He says that one who possesses such knowledge is indeed Śiva: "This [one]" (verse 21). Brahmā is the four-faced one (verses 22–25). There is no direct difference-in-identity with the Supreme Self—because difference and identity that are dependent [on conditions] possess specific attributes (saviśeṣatva)—[therefore] there is none (verses 26–28). "That which is without hands or feet," and so forth.
The meaning is that it belongs to the same section as the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad. || 29–35 ||
Truth and so forth are indeed the means for attaining the supreme knowledge;
such is the supreme knowledge, which is obtained through truth, austerity,
and virtues such as celibacy, by way of the path of the Vedānta.
Within their own bodies, those whose defects have been exhausted perceive the ultimate reality, which is the nature of self-luminous light; others, veiled by *māyā*, do not. (33)
For one who knows the Self, there is no going anywhere; likewise, for whichever yogi possesses this knowledge of the true nature [of reality],
there is no going anywhere, as he is of a complete form.
Just as the one, all-pervading space does not go anywhere, so too the supreme knower of the Self, which is Brahman, never goes anywhere. (35)
For the knower of Brahman, there is no such thing as "unfit food";
indeed, through the cessation of unfit food, the heart becomes pure.
When the food is pure, the purity of the mind follows naturally. (36)
When the mind is pure, knowledge arises gradually and the knots are clearly severed; however, for an embodied being devoid of the realization of Brahman, nothing is unfit to be consumed. (37)
Unlike that [ignorant person], the true nature of the possessor of right knowledge is indeed complete;
"I am the food, and I am always the eater of food"—this is the realization of Brahman. (38)
The knower of Brahman swallows everything through knowledge by means of the Self as Brahman;
for him, the entire order of Brahmans, Kshatriyas, and so forth, is always but food. (39)
Death is indeed the condiment for that which is such;
truly, through the realization of the nature of Brahman, the world becomes food. (40)
When the world appears as one's own self, then it becomes the object of enjoyment;
at that time, everything is eternally consumed as being one's own self, which is Brahman. (41)
When the world, as an object of enjoyment, appears in a certain form,
it certainly becomes consumed once it has appeared as one's own self through the means of valid cognition.
It enjoys its own essential nature by itself; there is no object of enjoyment separate from it.
If such a thing exists, it is of the nature of existence—Brahman alone, characterized by existence. (43)
Purity of food is the cause of knowledge for those who lack self-knowledge, by way of purifying the mind.
However, one who possesses self-knowledge swallows everything other than the Self as being nothing but the Self; thus he says: "Of that which is not to be eaten" (verse 36).
Through that [knowledge], knowledge arises and [karmic bonds] are severed (verses 37–45).
For the knower, the vision of his own identity with all things is existence characterized by being; that existence is Brahman and nothing else.
Apart from existence, there is nothing, and in reality, there is no such thing as māyā.
For yogis who are established in the Self, māyā is indeed imagined within the Self;
it appears in the form of a witness, but is sublated by the knowledge of Brahman. (45)
One who is perfected in the knowledge of Brahman, though constantly perceiving the entire world as manifest, never perceives it as separate from his own self. 46.
Thus ends the Upaniṣad.
Brahman, established through the negation of everything else, remains as its own non-dual self alone;
since nothing ever exists apart from it, the yogi endowed with the realization of Brahman perceives the entire universe— which appears only to the vision of the ignorant— as being nothing but that.

(248) Even though one may at times perceive [the world] as being like a mirage in the desert, one never perceives it as distinct from one’s own Self. The meaning is that, because Brahman alone is devoid of any counter-correlate (*niṣpratiyogika*), there is no room for the delusion that "there is" or "there is not" anything apart from Brahman. Thus ends the word *upaniṣad*.
This marks the conclusion of the present Upaniṣad.
This brief commentary on the Pāśupata Upaniṣad has been written by Upadeśabrahmayogin, the disciple of Śrī Vāsudevendra;
it is an exposition of the Pāśupata [Upaniṣad], adorned with two hundred verses.
Thus ends the commentary on the Pāśupata-Brahma-Upaniṣad, completing the seventy-seventh [treatise] in the illustrious exposition of the one hundred and eight Upaniṣads beginning with the Īśa.
